title: Why a dropped stone falls to the ground
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: Why do things fall down instead of up?
What pulls things to the ground?

explain.say: Every object with mass pulls on every other object. The Earth is so huge that its pull, called gravity, is strong enough to tug a stone straight down towards its centre.

draw.text: Why a dropped stone falls to the ground

explain.say: The pull of gravity on an object is its weight. When you let go of a stone, nothing is holding it up any more, so its weight makes it fall.
As the stone falls, air pushes up against it a little. For a small heavy stone this air resistance is tiny compared with its weight, so the stone keeps speeding up.
Near the ground, a falling stone speeds up by about 10 metres per second every second. Down everywhere on Earth means towards the centre, which is why people in Australia don't fall off.

faq.a: Gravity is the pull that every object with mass has on every other object. The more mass, the stronger the pull, so the giant Earth pulls everything near it towards its centre.
Yes, a little. Air pushes against anything moving through it. For a heavy compact stone the push is small, but for a light wide object like a leaf or a feather it is big enough to slow it a lot.
Without air in the way, a falling object gains about 9.8 metres per second of speed every second. After one second it is moving at about 10 metres per second, after two seconds about 20.
asks: How quickly does a dropped ball speed up?

faq.q: Why don't people on the other side of the Earth fall off?
faq.a: Because down means towards the centre of the Earth. Gravity pulls everyone, everywhere, towards the middle of the planet, so people in Australia are pulled onto the ground just like you.
asks: Why don't people in Australia fall off?

faq.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
faq.a: Mass is how much stuff is in an object, measured in kilograms. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, a force measured in newtons. On the Moon your mass stays the same but your weight is about one sixth.
asks: Is weight the same as mass?

facts: Near Earth's surface, gravity makes falling objects speed up by about 9.8 metres per second every second.
Isaac Newton described gravity as a pull between all masses in his book the Principia, published in 1687.
Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth as strong as on Earth.

quiz.say: You drop a stone from your hand. What makes it fall?

options.show: The Earth's gravity pulls it down
options.say: The Earth's gravity pulls it down

options.show: It wants to be near other stones
options.say: It wants to be near other stones

quiz.why: Gravity, the pull of the Earth's huge mass, pulls the stone towards the centre of the Earth.

wrong.0: Air actually pushes up against a falling object, slowing it slightly.
wrong.2: Stones don't want anything; the fall is caused by the force of gravity.
